title: Google, Anthropic and others to support new AI crawling opt-out standard
content:
Google, Anthropic and others to support new AI crawling opt-out standard
Google LLC, Microsoft Corp., Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to support an upcoming website crawling standard.
The technology will enable website operators to block artificial intelligence developers from using their content to train their models.
Many websites contain a text file titled “robots.txt” that informs crawlers what content they may access. A publisher can use the file to block scraping across the board or only make specific webpages inaccessible. It’s also possible to include certain other instructions. For example, a company can ask crawlers not to visit its website too often.
Website operators historically used robots.txt files to manage how search engines interact with their properties. Nowadays, the technology also helps regulate the activity of the scrapers with which AI providers collect training data.
A company that wishes to disallow training-related scraping must make multiple edits to its website’s robots.txt file. In particular, it needs to add a separate entry for every single AI provider. If an AI provider uses multiple scrapers to collect data, each scraper requires its own robots.txt entry.
The crawling standard Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI are backing aims to simplify the process. It would allow website operators to block all scrapers that collect training data for generative AI models with a single robots.txt entry. The setting wouldn’t apply to models that “perform exclusively non-generative tasks.”
The structure of robots.txt files follows a standardized format called the Robots Exclusion Protocol. Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI plan to incorporate their crawling standard into the format. They have already submitted a draft version of their proposal to the Internet Engineering Task Force, the nonprofit that maintains the Robots Exclusion Protocol.
Microsoft stated in a blog post that it will also provide a crawling setting called AI Grounding. It’s designed for situations where an AI model seeks to access a webpage in order to answer a user question rather than to collect training data.
Microsoft’s setting will enable website operators to prevent its services from sending such requests. The feature will also extend to third-party AI tools that use Microsoft technologies to process prompts.
OpenAI plans to offer similar controls. Both the ChatGPT developer and Microsoft intend to add support for the crawling standard in the coming months, while Google will follow suit sometime next year. Meta Platforms Inc. expressed support for the idea behind the technology but hasn’t yet committed to implementing it.

report.summary: Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI back a new robots.txt standard letting sites block AI training crawlers with one entry instead of per-provider lists.
report.background: For nearly three decades, robots.txt has been the web's informal handshake between site owners and crawlers, governed by the Robots Exclusion Protocol and maintained by the Internet Engineering Task Force. Originally built to manage search engine indexing, the file has been repurposed as the main defense against AI scraping since large language models turned public web pages into training data. The current approach is brittle: a publisher must add a separate entry for every AI vendor, and often for every distinct crawler a vendor operates, making opt-outs tedious and easy to get wrong. Meanwhile, legal fights and licensing deals have pushed the industry toward machine-readable consent signals. The new proposal, submitted as an IETF draft, tries to formalize that practice inside the existing standard rather than creating a parallel system.
key_points: One entry, all trainers: the proposed directive lets a site block every crawler gathering data for generative AI training with a single robots.txt rule, replacing the current patchwork of vendor-by-vendor lines and per-scraper entries that publishers must maintain and update manually.

Training is separated from answering: the opt-out applies only to generative training crawls, not to models doing 'exclusively non-generative tasks.' Microsoft is adding a companion 'AI Grounding' control so sites can also refuse requests made to answer a live user question rather than to build a dataset.

Rollout is staggered: Microsoft and OpenAI say support arrives in the coming months, Google targets sometime next year, and Meta has endorsed the concept without committing to ship it. That leaves a long window where enforcement is inconsistent across major vendors.

It is a convention, not a law: the standard is being folded into the Robots Exclusion Protocol via an IETF draft, which means compliance remains voluntary and unenforced, with no penalty for crawlers that simply ignore the file.
report.impact: For publishers and independent sites, the change cuts the cost of opting out from housekeeping to a single line, which should meaningfully expand who actually does it. For the AI industry, it formalizes a divide between licensed, crawled and blocked content, and pushes vendors toward separate infrastructure for training crawlers versus retrieval-time fetchers. Developers building on top of models should expect more gaps in training corpora and more refusals at inference time, and will need to honor these signals in their own agents and scrapers to avoid bad press and legal risk. Regular users are least visible but most affected downstream: model freshness on niche or paywalled topics may degrade as more sites opt out, while answer engines may cite fewer sources. Notably, the standard does nothing about payment, so licensing disputes remain unresolved.
report.tools: Worth watching: Dark Visitors (tracks which AI bots hit your site), Cloudflare's AI Crawl Control and bot management for enforcement, the open-source ai.robots.txt list and Spawning's Content Signals for ready-made directives, and robots.txt generators that support emerging directives. Follow the IETF HTTPAPI/ROBOTS draft for the exact syntax and Microsoft's AI Grounding documentation, which shows how retrieval-time blocking differs from training opt-outs in practice.
